money_at_stake.rationale: The occurrence's own claim scopes the money to 'the diesel and gas generator fleets clustered at data centers', not the whole data-center power buildout, so the band is anchored on the equipment market that permit class actually covers rather than on the much larger (and unrelated-in-cause) grid-interconnection story. Two independent market-research estimates for that specific equipment market bracket the same range: USD 10.34bn in 2026 (Fortune Business Insights, fetched directly this run) and USD 8.57bn in 2026 (MarketsandMarkets, fetched this run via a Yahoo Finance republication of the same dated press release after the original GlobeNewswire URL failed to load on three separate attempts). Both sit comfortably inside B1_10 and neither is close to a band boundary, so the estimates disagreeing by about 20% does not change the call. Deliberately NOT widened to the full behind-the-meter gas-turbine build, whose scale is evidenced separately under public_reach and capture_odds (GE Vernova's growing gas-turbine backlog and rising pricing): that larger build is driven mainly by grid-interconnection delays, of which this specific minor-source permitting rule is one contributing bottleneck among several, and no fetched source ties a dollar figure to the slice this rule alone unlocks. Scoring the narrower, directly-named pool avoids putting an invented attribution at the head of the funnel. (Amended 2026-08-30 second pass: two unsourced figures used only as color in the prior draft of this rationale, a single-quarter GE Vernova electrification-order total and an industry-wide behind-the-meter gigawatt figure, were removed because no fetched source was found to support either; removing them changes no score.)

public_reach.rationale: This is close to the mirror image of the Arctic occurrence's finding. The named suppliers of the exact equipment class this occurrence is about (diesel and gas backup/prime gensets for data centers) are, with one clearly-identified exception, listed or subsidiaries of listed groups: Caterpillar (NYSE: CAT, 18% share) and Cummins (NYSE: CMI, 16% share) hold roughly a third of the market between them. Fortune Business Insights' own top-players list for this market also names Atlas Copco (listed, Nasdaq Stockholm), Generac Power Systems (NYSE: GNRC), Kohler, Mitsubishi Corporation (listed, Tokyo), ABB (listed, SIX/NYSE), and three smaller specialists, Eurodiesel Services, HITECH Power Protection and Aksa Power Generation, whose listing status this appraisal did not independently verify. Kohler is the one clearly-identified private major holdout. On the adjacent gas-turbine tier of on-site generation that the same permit class increasingly also covers for larger installations, GE Vernova (NYSE: GEV) is listed and reports data-center-tied demand explicitly by name: its gas-turbine backlog grew from 83 GW at year-end 2025 to 100 GW in the first quarter of 2026 to 116 GW by the second quarter, and management states roughly 20% of its gas-turbine customers are data-center operators against 80% traditional utilities. Not scored above 85 because the demand side, the data-center operators who pay for and site this equipment, is genuinely mixed (listed REITs and hyperscalers alongside large private capital), so the occurrence's reach is asymmetric: overwhelmingly public on the supply side, mixed on the demand side. (Amended 2026-08-30 second pass: this rationale previously named Rolls-Royce as one of Fortune Business Insights' listed players and asserted Siemens Energy explicitly reports data-center order growth by name; on refetching, Fortune Business Insights' own player list does not include Rolls-Royce and no fetched source was found naming Siemens Energy's data-center orders specifically, so both claims were removed. It also previously asserted Kohler is confined mostly to sub-1MW output, which the fetched source does not state; that specific claim was removed and Kohler is described only as the clearly-identified private holdout. None of these three removals changes the score, since the underlying finding, CAT and CMI dominate a segment that is otherwise almost entirely listed, is unaffected.)

capture_odds.rationale: Two independent, dated signals point the same direction: the suppliers, not their customers, are holding the leverage right now. GE Vernova reported its gas-turbine backlog growing from 83 GW at year-end 2025 to 100 GW in the first quarter of 2026, with pricing rising faster than inflation and management describing 10-20% price growth on new bidding and winning activity versus the prior backlog. Industry-wide lead times on the exact hardware class this occurrence names (large standby diesel gensets, medium-voltage switchgear) have roughly doubled to tripled versus the pre-2020 norm: 52+ weeks versus a 16-24 week pre-2020 baseline for standby diesel, and up to 72 weeks versus roughly 24 weeks pre-2020 for switchgear. That combination, rising price alongside lengthening queues, is consistent with suppliers holding pricing power rather than being pure price-takers. Not scored higher because the segment this occurrence actually names (diesel/gas gensets) has more competing suppliers than the narrower utility-scale gas-turbine tier where the strongest pricing-power evidence (GE Vernova) actually comes from; full concentration-based pricing power is better evidenced for the turbine tier than for the genset tier this occurrence is centered on. Revised down from the first pass (76) on this second pass: that draft cited a third corroborating example, a Cummins Fridley, Minnesota capacity-expansion announcement, that could not be independently verified this run (its only cited source, a blog, was unreachable across repeated attempts and the Wayback Machine is unreachable from this tool; a Cummins SEC 8-K found by search returned HTTP 403). That item was deleted rather than repaired with a weaker source. The two surviving, independently fetched items still support the same direction, but the evidence base is thinner than three corroborating examples, which the score now reflects.

timing_fit.rationale: The occurrence's own dated facts (EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-1212, published in the Federal Register 2026-07-07, comments closed 2026-08-21) are now independently corroborated by two fetched, unaffiliated outlets: EarthTimes confirms the comment-close date and the Georgia permit statistic verbatim, and WorldHab confirms the exact docket number and the Federal Register citation (91 FR 41591) verbatim. That cuts both ways for timing. In favor: the money this rule would accelerate is not speculative future capex, it is already being spent now on the supply side regardless of when, or whether, this specific rule finalizes, evidenced by Caterpillar's Power Generation segment sales rising 41% year over year in the first quarter of 2026 on demand it names as primarily data-center applications, and by GE Vernova's gas-turbine backlog and pricing both rising over the same period (evidenced under capture_odds). Against: the occurrence itself, the specific procedural unlock (removing the federal public-comment floor), has no committed finalization date in any source found, and EPA Clean Air Act rulemakings of this kind commonly take many months to over a year past comment close, with real litigation risk given active Sierra Club opposition already on the public record. Scored above the 30 anchor because the underlying spend is dated and moving now; not scored at 85 because the rule's own contribution to that spend, versus the secular interconnection-delay driver already in motion, has no committed date and is contestable. (Amended 2026-08-30 second pass: the prior draft's sole corroborating source for the occurrence's own dates, The Register, was checked against its actual fetched text and found to state none of the dates, the docket ID, or the Georgia figure it was cited for; that item is deleted, not repaired, and replaced with the two sources above, independently found and fetched this run. The prior draft's Caterpillar evidence also claimed the company's Power Generation order book 'extends into 2028'; the fetched press release contains no such statement, so that specific claim is dropped and only the confirmed 41% sales-growth figure is retained. Score held at 62: the underlying reasoning is unchanged and the replacement sourcing is, if anything, more precise than what it replaces.)

REACHABLE, not LEAKY: this occurrence inverts the Arctic finding. The equipment side of this chain (gensets and gas turbines) is overwhelmingly listed and shows real, dated pricing leverage; the open question a chain build should resolve is capture depth per named issuer (CAT and CMI dominate the genset tier at 34% combined share; GEV and Siemens Energy the adjacent turbine tier) rather than whether the money reaches a brokerage account at all. Start a chain build from the equipment-supply side, not from data-center operator names, since the operators are the mixed listed/private demand side this appraisal explicitly did not credit toward public_reach. Flag for the chain build: the specific regulatory unlock this occurrence names has no committed finalization date and carries litigation risk, so the timing case should be built on the already-committed supplier order books, not on an assumption that this EPA rule finalizes on any particular schedule.
